content: Glutelins are a class of proteins that are soluble in dilute acids, bases, detergents, chaotropic agents, or reducing agents. These proteins are generally similar to prolamins and are found in certain grass seeds. Among the glutelins, glutenin is the most commonly encountered, particularly in wheat, where it plays a critical role in imparting the refined baking properties characteristic of bread wheat. Glutelins have also been identified in barley and rye. In these species, glutelins are typically categorized into high molecular weight (HMW) and low molecular weight (LMW) forms. During the baking process, these proteins form cross-links with themselves and other proteins through disulfide bonds, contributing to the structural and functional properties of the dough. A specific HMW glutelin, known as glutenin, found in the grass tribe Triticeae, can act as a sensitizing agent for individuals with celiac disease. This occurs in individuals who carry the HLA-DQ8 class II antigen receptor gene, making them susceptible to an immune response triggered by this protein.
